app.name: Vacuon
app.readOnlyNotice: Vacuon sets items aside by default, into a quarantine you can restore from; the Recycle Bin and permanent deletion are both a separate, explicit choice. Purging a batch is the only step that cannot be undone.

elevation.notElevatedHint: Not elevated — the scan will use the Windows API (slower)

elevation.alwaysOn: Vacuon will relaunch elevated every time you open it. Windows shows the UAC prompt — there is no way to suppress it without creating a scheduled task, and that is not done behind your back.
elevation.alwaysOff: Turn on to always open elevated. Without elevation there is no MFT read, and the scan goes from seconds to minutes.
elevation.whyBody: Reading the MFT means opening the volume in raw mode (\\.\C:), and only an elevated process may do that. It is the difference between indexing a million files in seconds and taking minutes through the Windows API. Vacuon opens the volume for READING only — never for writing.

security.title: Registry persistence points
security.intro: 44 keys where malware commonly takes root: Run and RunOnce, Winlogon, AppInit_DLLs, AppCertDlls, Image File Execution Options, SilentProcessExit, LSA packages, Command Processor, Active Setup, BHOs, file associations and the Startup folder.
security.disclaimer: Read-only — no key is modified. Vacuon is not an antivirus: there is no signature database here, only behavioural heuristics with the reason always in plain sight. Legitimate entries do show up in the list; read the why before concluding anything.
security.prompt: Inspects 44 registry points where malware commonly takes root. Read-only — nothing is changed.
security.emptyHint: Click Inspect. Without administrator rights, protected HKLM keys and the Scheduled Tasks are left out — and the report says exactly that instead of passing the list off as complete.

security.experimentalBody: This module is the newest part of Vacuon and the least settled. It has no signature database — only behavioural rules — and on an elevated full-volume scan it reaches files a normal scan never sees, so the count can be high. Treat every finding as “worth a look”, never as a verdict, and do not delete anything on its word alone.
security.falsePositiveNote: A false positive here is treated as a bug. If something legitimate shows up, please report it.

memory.title: What is using this machine's memory
memory.intro: Measured now, grouped by program and ranked by private memory — the figure that answers who is actually holding the RAM.
memory.honestyNote: Working set is what Task Manager shows, and it counts pages shared between processes once for each of them, so adding it up across a browser's children gives a total larger than the machine has. Private memory is the one that adds up.
memory.prompt: Click Inspect to measure. Nothing is changed until you ask.
memory.compressedNote: Pages Windows compressed and kept in memory instead of writing them to disk. It looks like waste in a process list and is the opposite — it is the reason those pages did not become disk reads.
memory.load: {0}% in use, as Windows reports it
memory.fromStartupTotal: {0} of what is in use belongs to programs Windows launches at sign-in. Turning one off in Startup removes it for good; nothing on this screen can.
memory.trimExplain: This is the button other utilities call "free memory". It empties working sets, and the available figure goes up — but nothing was freed. The pages moved to the standby list or the pagefile and come back, from disk, the moment their program touches them again. On a machine that is not short of memory it usually makes things slower, not faster.
memory.trimResult: {0} processes trimmed · available moved by {1}. Those pages went to disk or standby, and return when their programs need them.
memory.trimResultNegative: {0} processes trimmed · available actually went DOWN by {1}. Windows pulled pages back in. This is what the number looks like when nobody rounds it in their favour.
memory.closeProtected: Windows needs this one; Vacuon will not close it
memory.closed: Closed. It was holding {0}, and available memory rose by {1}.
memory.closedPartial: {0} of {1} processes closed. They were holding {2}, and available memory rose by {3}.
memory.closeDenied: Access denied — that process runs at a higher level than Vacuon. Restart elevated and try again.
memory.closeStillRunning: The close was issued and the process is still there. Nothing is being claimed.

ai.title: Microsoft AI components
ai.intro: Windows ships a number of AI features, and turns several of them on without asking. This tab reads the state of each one and can switch off the ones Microsoft documents a control for.
ai.disclaimer: Only Microsoft components appear here. Third-party AI software on this machine is none of this tab's business, however much of it there is.
ai.honestyNote: Vacuon writes the documented value and reads it back to confirm it is there. Whether Windows acts on it right away or only after you sign out is up to Windows, and this tab will not claim otherwise.
ai.journalNote: Every change is written to {0} before the registry is touched, so Undo always has something to restore.

ai.outcomeUndone: Put back the way it was found.
ai.outcomeNoChange: Already in that state; nothing was written.
ai.outcomeNeedsElevation: This one lives under HKLM and needs Administrator. Restart elevated and try again.
ai.outcomeNotConfirmed: The write went through but reading it back did not return it. Nothing is being claimed.

cli.cmdSimilarVideo: Videos that are the same footage, re-encoded or resized
similar.fromCache: {0} came from the stored fingerprints, so they were not decoded again.
similarVideo.scope: {0} videos to read, {1} in all. Frames are decoded from each one, so this takes minutes rather than seconds.

similarVideo.tooShort: {0} were shorter than {1} seconds. Sampling five moments out of a few seconds returns five views of one instant.

cli.cmdResidue: Folders left behind by programs that are no longer installed
cli.cmdCompress: Folders NTFS would compress well, that are not compressed

residue.read: Read {0} installed programs and examined {1} folders.
residue.guess: Every line above is a guess made by comparing names against the Windows uninstall list, and a name is not an identity. Anything installed outside that list — npm and pnpm tools, scoop, portable apps — will ALWAYS look unclaimed and appear here while still in use. Nothing was deleted. Check each one before you remove it.
compress.none: No folder here is worth compressing.
compress.estimate: Those figures are ESTIMATES: bytes times a ratio typical of the file type, not a trial compression of these files. Everything else Vacuon prints was measured; this was not.
compress.howTo: Vacuon compresses nothing. Use `compact /c /s` in the folder, or its Properties dialog.
diff.needsVolume: This compares whole volumes, so it needs a drive letter rather than a folder.
diff.needsElevation: Comparing scans needs Administrator: the snapshot is keyed by the NTFS volume serial, which is in the volume metadata.
diff.noBaseline: There is no earlier scan of this volume to compare against. This run did not create one either — scan the volume once and the next run will have something to measure from.
diff.window: {0} between the two scans, and the volume went {1} overall.
diff.nothing: No folder moved by more than {0}.
diff.folders: Folders, not files: matching files across two scans means tracking them through renames and MFT record reuse, and getting that wrong reports one file as both created and deleted.
